summary.text: A 36-year-old woman (gravida 0, para 0) presented with abdominal pain. She had undergone a right salpingo-oophorectomy for an ovarian endometrioma 16 years earlier. Five years before presentation laparoscopic surgery for a recurrent left ovarian endometrioma was aborted because of severe adhesions. The cyst reached 7 cm and a left ovarian cystectomy by laparotomy was performed. Persistent postoperative pain was treated with a GnRH antagonist for 3 months. Two months before presentation she was hospitalized with lower abdominal pain and fever and was diagnosed with PID and an endometrioma with abscess.

MRI showed a left ovarian endometrioma adherent to the sigmoid colon with a tear-drop-shaped T2FS lesion whose narrow portion extended into the colon lumen; no fatty component was seen and teratoma was ruled out. CT around the same time showed a 6-cm left adnexal cystic mass containing intralesional air, suggesting a possible communication between intestine and ovary. All cases were associated with endometriosis.

Because of the risks of surgical castration and bowel perforation, she received the GnRH antagonist relugolix 40 mg/day for 6 months, followed by dienogest 2 mg/day. Her symptoms remained stable for a period of 9 months, and the authors state that symptoms in Cases 1 and 2 were successfully managed conservatively.

summary.text: A 42-year-old woman (gravida 1, para 1) presented with dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain and a one-week history of fever and did not complain of bowel-related symptoms. On T2-weighted MRI a high-intensity area appeared to extend from the cyst toward the colo-rectal lumen, and MRI showed free air within the left ovarian endometrioma. All cases were associated with endometriosis.

Antibiotic treatment was administered and her symptoms improved. A follow-up MRI performed 1 month later revealed that the free air had resolved. She was then managed expectantly without any medication for 9 months, with no recurrence of PID symptoms during this period; the authors state that symptoms in Cases 1 and 2 were successfully managed conservatively.

summary.text: A 42-year-old woman (gravida 2, para 0) with no significant medical history developed dysmenorrhea and severe anemia nine years before presentation and was diagnosed with adenomyosis. Four years before presentation her dysmenorrhea worsened and she was admitted; infertility treatment was not feasible because of severe anemia, a GnRH agonist was administered, and infertility treatment was later discontinued.

She underwent hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy to relieve symptoms. Preoperative MRI showed diffuse adenomyosis but no ovarian cysts. At surgery the uterus was enlarged with diffuse adenomyosis and multiple myomas and dense adhesions surrounded the left ovary, which were partially dissected while the recto-sigmoid adhesions were left untouched. Pathology confirmed adenomyosis and leiomyoma without malignancy.

The postoperative course was initially uneventful, but on postoperative day 2 she developed fever, abdominal pain and peritonitis, and symptoms worsened despite antibiotics. CT showed a low-density area raising suspicion for rectal perforation. Emergent laparotomy found the left ovary densely adherent to the recto-sigmoid colon, and a leak test showed air leaking from the ovary surface, leading to the conclusion of a fistula between intestine and ovary.

En bloc resection of the affected sigmoid colon and left ovary followed by colostomy was performed. The resected specimen showed a fistulous tract from the intestinal mucosa into the ovary, with the ruptured intestinal segment covered by the ovary and no features of mechanical injury; pathology showed a subserosal diverticulum and endometriosis in the surrounding mucosa. The colostomy was closed within 3 months.

Case 3 discussion says no evidence of ovarian involvement, which conflicts with the case text describing a tract into the ovary; recorded as a review-only item.
Case 3 resection and colostomy are recorded as a decision in the case text; surgical treatment is recorded from the abstract and discussion.
Retrospective author scenarios and suspected mechanisms (sealed fistula, diverticulum overlap) are kept as review-only or ambiguity entries.
Discussion statements about MRI and CT free air in Cases 1 and 2 are kept as separate observations from the case-text findings.
